title: Nine Tips for More Energy
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart shares nine practices he adopted over a summer to protect his energy for work, family and play, drawing on Jim Collins, Make Time, Dan Pink and Brigid Schulte. The tips include chipping away at sleep debt in small nightly increments, using a coffee-then-nap routine, logging daily energy like a researcher studying himself, and keeping a list of people who energize you. He also advises taking real breaks instead of digital ones, building in daily quiet, delaying and limiting caffeine, and exercising about twenty minutes a day without overdoing it. The framing move is that simple rules do not drain life but create freedom and creative output, and that tending energy is a way to increase one's usefulness to others. It is a personal-habits list for professionals rather than a classroom piece.
points: Sleep debt is better repaid in small nightly additions than in a single long catch-up night, a habit Jim Collins tracks by totaling recent hours.
Self-observation, such as a daily note on sleep, caffeine, food and exercise, lets a professional learn where energy actually comes from.
Fake breaks like email and social feeds trade one demanding mental task for another, while real breaks use movement, quiet or rest.
Constant audio stimulation contributes to overwhelm, so scheduled quiet is treated as a recovery practice.
Stuart argues that a few simple rules about energy produce more freedom and give him more to offer others.
quotes: Chip away at sleep debt rather than trying to pay it off one morning a week. It’s better to add 30 minutes to each night of sleep for a week than to add 4 hours to one night of sleep once per week.
Nappucinos work. This is the thing where right before that afternoon slump hits, you down a cup of coffee and then lay down and shut your eyes for fifteen minutes.
Treat yourself like an organism that you are studying. Jim Collins used to keep a “bug book” on himself, studying himself to try to understand what he should do with his life.
I wouldn’t like to see the number of times that I’ve taken a “break” from work by checking email or Twitter or the news or YouTube. This is dumb.
Instead, take a walk, do some jumping jacks, stare at a window, do a nappucino, call your grandma… do something besides the digital default.

Thanks to headphones and podcasts and Spotify and car radio and audiobooks, it’s easy to ensure that every moment of our day is filled with stimuli. I’ve found it quite liberating to intentionally not use stimuli at various points in the day.

All of these can seem a bit nit-picky when you look at them, like a list of buzz-killing joy-stealers. But I’ve found the opposite to be true: when I operate beneath a few simple, logical rules like these, I end up experiencing more freedom and creative output, and I end up giving more to others.
